en: Beholding the citizens of the city— women and men— who were like figures in a painting, well-dressed and adorned with golden ornaments,
he reflected, "I have seen them myself in person," and took his pleasure with them.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the initiation of the Guru, does not succumb to delusion. || 1 ||
In the forest, beholding trees with their beautiful tops bent low under the weight of fruits and flowers,
covered in dense shade and filled with flocks of birds warbling loudly,
he spent his nights reclining on the bare ground as his sole bed.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
Sometimes dwelling in a palace, sometimes in the mansions of the wealthy; at times on a mountain, sometimes on the banks of rivers;
and even residing in the huts of the most excellent sages who have subdued their senses.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
In one place, he laughs along with children who clap their hands; in another, he sports with young women adorned by their youth;
and in yet another, he laments with the elderly whose hearts are agitated by anxiety.
The sage, whose darkness has been utterly destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
Sometimes by learned scholars and seekers of knowledge intensely devoted [to truth], sometimes by eminent poets who are masters of the essence of poetic figures and sentiments,
and sometimes by the best of logicians intent on inference through sound reasoning;
The sage, whose darkness has been utterly destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.

When, with a delighted mind and intent on prostration, shall I perform worship for the Lord— sometimes through the practice of meditation, sometimes with fragrant, blossoming, and excellent flowers, and at other times with pure leaves alone?
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.

When indeed has one ever recited the garland of names of Śivā, or of Śambhu, or even of Viṣṇu, or of the Lord of the Gaṇas who has manifested his supreme boons— while the rivers of bliss flow from the eyes?
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
When shall I perform my ablutions— sometimes with the waters of the Gaṅgā, sometimes with water drawn from a well, sometimes with that from a pond, sometimes with warm water, sometimes with cold,
and sometimes with ashes white as camphor?
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
Sometimes he remains awake, engaging with objects through the sense organs; sometimes he experiences even the objects of the dream state;
and sometimes he constantly experiences the bliss of deep sleep.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
Sometimes clothed in hope, sometimes wearing divine garments, and sometimes even bearing upon his waist the skin of a lion;

The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the initiation of the Guru, does not succumb to delusion. || 10 ||
Sometimes abiding in goodness, sometimes functioning through passion, O Sugata; sometimes functioning through darkness, and elsewhere again free from all three;
sometimes a transmigrating being, and sometimes dwelling on the path of sacred revelation—oh! [how varied is Your manifestation].
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
Sometimes remaining in silence, and sometimes engaged in the utterance of speech; sometimes abandoning words in the impetuous joy of laughter at his own bliss;
and sometimes intent on observing the worldly activities of people.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the initiation of his guru, does not succumb to delusion.
Sometimes, casting a lotus into the blossoming lotus-faces of the Śaktis, and sometimes taking it back from his own mouth himself,
he manifested that non-dual form which is devoid of self and other.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the initiation of his guru, does not succumb to delusion. || 13 ||
Sometimes dwelling with followers of Śiva, sometimes with followers of Śakti; sometimes dwelling with devotees of Viṣṇu, and sometimes with devotees of Sūrya;
at other times with the attendants of Gaṇeśa—having transcended all distinctions through non-duality.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
At times beholding his own stainless Śiva-nature as formless, and at other times as manifold and pure through the differentiation of various qualities with form,
he is sometimes struck with wonder, thinking "What is this?", and at other times he is filled with joy.
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.
When, through the power of the repeated realization of the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), one perceives even the entire world of duality as being truly composed of Śiva,
and having transcended the appearance of duality, one utters only "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva"— then [one attains liberation].
The sage, whose darkness has been destroyed by the guru’s initiation, does not succumb to delusion.

If an excellent man, through his meritorious deeds, daily immerses himself again and again in this state of liberation— which abides in supreme Śiva, is attained through the nectar-like glances of the Guru's grace, and is a pool of innate bliss— he attains it.
Then, the wise here say that he is a renouncer, a yogi, and a poet. || 17 ||
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
The Wave of Bliss of Liberation while Living is complete.
